name: Toyota
blurb: The best-selling carmaker on Earth. Built its name on durability, then proved it could do excitement too, the 2000GT, the Supra, and a Land Cruiser that outlasts its owners.

name: Corolla
intro: The best-selling nameplate in history, more than 50 million sold. The Corolla is the default answer to 'what car should I buy?' on every continent, and the GR Corolla proves the badge can still have a pulse.
photoCredit: Photo: TTTNIS, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Camry
intro: America's best-selling sedan for over two decades. The Camry is the car as appliance done perfectly, and since 2024, hybrid-only, which tells you where the whole segment went.
photoCredit: Photo: Throwawayacc222, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Supra
intro: Four generations of inline-six grand tourer, one legend: the Mk IV's 2JZ engine became the most famous tuning platform on Earth. The name returned in 2019, co-developed with BMW.
photoCaption: Supra A80 (Mk IV), modified example, Hong Kong street
photoCredit: Photo: Dinkun Chen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Land Cruiser
intro: The vehicle that goes where roads apologize. From the FJ40 to the 300 Series, the Land Cruiser is the expedition default on every continent, the car aid workers and armies trust when failure isn't an option.
photoCredit: Photo: Johannes Maximilian, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Prius
intro: The car that made 'hybrid' a word your parents knew. The second generation became a cultural symbol; the fifth became, improbably, genuinely good-looking.
photoCredit: Photo: TTTNIS, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Tacoma
intro: The midsize truck benchmark for resale value and trail credibility. Tacomas are bought, used hard for a decade, and sold for embarrassing fractions of their original price.
photoCaption: 2024 Toyota Tacoma TRD Off Road black rear
photoCredit: Photo: Throwawayacc222, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: 2000GT
intro: Japan's first supercar. Co-developed with Yamaha, hand-built in tiny numbers, 351 cars, and proof in 1967 that Japan could build a world-class GT. A Bond film made one a convertible because Sean Connery didn't fit.
photoCredit: Photo: MrWalkr, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Honda
blurb: An engine company that happens to build cars. VTEC, the NSX, and a Civic for every budget and every era of a driver's life.

name: Civic
intro: Started as a fuel-crisis runabout and grew into the compact benchmark. Every generation has had a version worth caring about, and the Type R versions are among the best front-drive cars ever made.
photoCaption: 2022 Honda Civic LX Sedan, front right, 11-02-2022
photoCredit: Photo: MercurySable99, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Accord
intro: The family sedan for people who actually read reviews. The Accord spent decades trading best-in-class wins with the Camry, and usually won on steering and feel rather than on price.
photoCaption: 2007 Honda Accord Euro R with Mugen tuning front
photoCredit: Photo: Throwawayacc222, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: NSX
intro: The supercar that embarrassed Ferrari on reliability and usability, then came back 25 years later as a hybrid. Ayrton Senna helped develop the first one. That fact alone tells you the intent.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: S2000
intro: A 9,000 rpm love letter to the naturally aspirated engine. The F20C made 120 hp per litre, a record for a production road car at launch, and the shifter is still the benchmark every manual is judged against.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: CR-V
intro: One of the original car-based crossovers, and still the sensible default in the segment. It has never been exciting. It has also never really been beaten at the job it was built for.
photoCaption: 2023 Honda CR-V EX-L 4WD in Radiant Red Metallic, rear right
photoCredit: Photo: Mr.choppers, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Nissan
blurb: Home of Godzilla. The GT-R line spent five decades embarrassing supercars, and the Z car made performance democratic.

name: GT-R
intro: Nissan's giant-killer, built for 17 years with one brief: be faster than cars costing three times as much. It mostly was. All-wheel drive, a hand-built twin-turbo V6, and a launch-control party trick that never got old.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Z
intro: The people's sports car, running since 1969 with a long nap in the middle. The 240Z made performance democratic; the current car keeps the twin-turbo, rear-drive, manual-gearbox faith alive when most rivals dropped it.
photoCaption: 1991 Nissan Fairlady Z 300ZX 2by2 Twin Turbo in Platinum Mist Metallic, front right (Queen Street 2023)
photoCredit: Photo: Elise240SX, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Skyline GT-R
intro: Three generations of Skyline GT-R that never officially came to America, which only sharpened the legend. The RB26 engine's official 276 hp was a gentlemen's-agreement fiction everyone politely maintained.
photoCredit: Photo: User3204, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Leaf
intro: The car that proved ordinary people would buy an electric car if it was priced like a car. First-generation cars depreciate like dropped phones, which makes a healthy-battery example one of the cheapest ways to run a second car there is.
photoCaption: Nissan Leaf - Mondial de l'Automobile de Paris 2012 - 006
photoCredit: Photo: Thesupermat, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Patrol
intro: Land Cruiser's oldest rival, and in much of the Middle East and Australia, the preferred one. The Patrol is what UN fleets and desert drivers buy when a breakdown is not a survivable option.
photoCredit: Photo: OSX, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Mazda
blurb: The small company that bet on rotary engines and lightweight roadsters when nobody else would. The MX-5 is the best-selling two-seat sports car in history.

name: MX-5 Miata
intro: The best-selling two-seat sports car in history, and the answer to almost any 'what fun car should I buy?' question. Power was never the point. Response, weight, and a roof that drops in seconds always were.
photoCredit: Photo: Chris Woodrich, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: RX-7
intro: The rotary engine's masterpiece. Three generations, one idea: light weight and an engine that revs like a motorcycle. The FD is the famous one; the earlier cars are the honest bargains.
photoCredit: Photo: TTTNIS, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Mazda3
intro: The compact for people who notice steering feel. Mazda kept giving the 3 a better interior and sharper chassis than the segment required, and the current turbo AWD car is nearly a luxury product wearing a mainstream badge.
photoCaption: Mazda3 Fastback e-SKYACTIV X AWD (front three-quarter view) at Mazda Museum
photoCredit: Photo: Aos.1905, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: CX-5
intro: The crossover that proved family cars didn't have to steer like appliances. The CX-5 built Mazda's modern business, the profits from this car fund everything else the company makes.
photoCaption: Mazda CX-5 - Mondial de l'Automobile de Paris 2012 - 001
photoCredit: Photo: Thesupermat, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Subaru
blurb: All-wheel drive and boxer engines, everywhere, always. Rally stages made the WRX a legend; the Outback made wagons into a lifestyle.

name: Impreza WRX
intro: Rally car for the road, in continuous production in spirit since 1992. Turbo flat-four, all-wheel drive, and a bonnet scoop you could set your watch by. The STI versions are modern classics; the plain WRX is just a great all-weather fast car.
photoCaption: WRX STI (VA), rally-prepared example in competition livery
photoCredit: Photo: Yu Chu Chin, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Outback
intro: The wagon that out-SUV'd the SUVs. Subaru jacked up a Legacy, added cladding, and accidentally created the blueprint for half the cars on American roads today, while never giving up the wagon part.
photoCaption: 2018 Subaru Outback SE Premium Symmetrical CVT 2.5 Front
photoCredit: Photo: Vauxford, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: BRZ
intro: Proof a sports car doesn't need power, it needs balance. Subaru built the flat-four and the chassis; Toyota handled much of the rest. The result is the car driving instructors and racers agree on.
photoCredit: Photo: Tokumeigakarinoaoshima, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Forester
intro: The tall, boxy, all-weather wagon-SUV that Vermont runs on. Early turbo XTs are cult cars; later ones are simply the sensible answer for snow-belt families who refuse to buy a crossover that looks like an egg.
photoCredit: Photo: TTTNIS, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Hyundai
blurb: The fastest climb in the industry, from budget punchline in the 1990s to design-led EVs and the N performance division that embarrasses hot hatches twice its price.

name: Elantra
intro: Hyundai's compact started as transport for people who couldn't afford a Civic and ended up producing the Elantra N, one of the best performance bargains on sale. That arc is Hyundai's last 30 years in miniature.
photoCredit: Photo: Crisco 1492, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Sonata
intro: The car that announced Hyundai could design. The 2011 Sonata's swooping styling forced every midsize rival to follow, and the current car splits its personality between efficient hybrids and a properly quick N Line.
photoCredit: Photo: Benespit, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Ioniq 5
intro: A retro-futuristic hatchback the size of a crossover, and the car that made Hyundai a design leader in the EV era. Pixel lights, a flat floor, and charging speeds that embarrassed cars costing twice as much at launch.
photoCaption: Hyundai Ioniq 5, rear 3/4, at a dealer
photoCredit: Photo: Alexander-93, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Tucson
intro: Hyundai's RAV4 and CR-V rival, and the model that shows how far the mainstream range has come: the current hybrid is efficient, quick enough, and styled like it escaped from a motor show stand.
photoCredit: Photo: UltraTech66, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Ford
blurb: Put the world on wheels with the Model T, then gave it the Mustang and the F-Series. The company that beat Ferrari at Le Mans out of spite.

name: Model T
intro: The car that put the world on wheels. Ford built over 15 million of them, cut the price from $850 to under $300, and in doing so invented the moving assembly line's reason to exist. By the early 1920s, roughly half the cars on Earth were Model Ts.
photoCaption: Ford Model T touring car, brass-era example, museum display
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Mustang
intro: Launched in April 1964 and sold 22,000 cars on day one. The Mustang invented the pony car, long hood, short deck, endless options list, and has survived gas crises, the Mustang II, and the SUV era without ever leaving production.
photoCredit: Photo: Matti Blume, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: F-Series (F-150)
intro: America's best-selling vehicle line for over four decades. The F-Series is less a model than an economy, work truck, family hauler, off-road toy, and status symbol, all on the same ladder frame.
photoCaption: Ford F-Series XII SVT Raptor Crew Cab China 2012-04-15
photoCredit: Photo: Navigator84, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: GT (GT40 lineage)
intro: One nameplate, three separate vendettas against physics. The GT40 was built to beat Ferrari at Le Mans after Enzo walked away from selling to Ford, and did it four years straight, 1966 to 1969. Both modern revivals exist because that grudge never cooled.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Bronco
intro: Ford's answer to the Jeep CJ in 1966, a full-size truck-based SUV by the 1980s, dead in 1996, and revived in 2021 as a removable-roof Wrangler rival. The first-generation trucks are the collector sweet spot; the new one is the one you can actually use daily.
photoCredit: Photo: AHHNiewohner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Chevrolet
blurb: GM's volume brand and America's performance bargain. The Corvette has been the attainable supercar since 1953; the small-block V8 powered everything.

name: Corvette
intro: America's attainable supercar since 1953. The Corvette's trick has always been the arithmetic: most of a European exotic's speed for a fraction of the price. The C8's move to a mid-engine layout in 2020 broke a 67-year tradition and nobody sensible misses the old one.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Camaro
intro: GM's answer to the Mustang, launched for 1967 and locked in the pony-car war for six generations. Production ended again in 2024 with no successor announced, the sixth generation went out as the best-driving Camaro ever made.
photoCredit: Photo: Kevauto, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Silverado
intro: Chevrolet's full-size truck and Ford's oldest argument. Chevrolet pickups go back to 1918, but the Silverado nameplate dates to 1999, when it replaced the C/K line. The 3.0L Duramax diesel is the connoisseur's pick; the 6.2L V8 is the loud one.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Bel Air
intro: Chevrolet's top trim line through the 1950s, and the 1955–1957 'Tri-Five' cars are about as close as American design gets to universal agreement. The '57 Bel Air is shorthand for the whole decade.
photoCaption: Chevrolet Bel Air (1953).- Carmel by the sea, California USA
photoCredit: Photo: Pierre André Leclercq, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Impala
intro: Chevrolet's flagship nameplate from 1958, and the best-selling car in America through the mid-1960s, over a million sold in 1965 alone. It lived three lives: the 1960s icon, the 1990s Impala SS sleeper, and a competent front-drive sedan until 2020.
photoCredit: Photo: Ermell, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Jeep
blurb: Born for war, kept for weekends. The Wrangler is the direct descendant of the Willys MB, and the seven-slot grille is the most copied face in off-roading.

name: Wrangler
intro: The direct descendant of the Willys MB that won a war, carried through the CJ line and renamed Wrangler in 1987. Solid axles, a folding windshield, doors that come off, the formula has survived four corporate owners because altering it would end the business.
photoCredit: Photo: Dinkun Chen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Grand Cherokee
intro: The SUV that took Jeep upmarket. The Grand Cherokee created the premium 4x4 niche in 1993, proper off-road hardware under a vehicle you'd park at a hotel, and Range Rover has been answering it ever since.
photoCredit: Photo: IFCAR, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

name: CJ (Civilian Jeep)
intro: CJ stands for Civilian Jeep, the Willys MB demobbed in 1945 and sold to farmers, surveyors, and anyone who needed to get somewhere roads didn't go. The CJ-5 alone ran for 29 years, and every Wrangler since is this shape with better manners.
photoCredit: Photo: dave_7 from Lethbridge, Canada, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Wagoneer
intro: The original luxury SUV. The SJ Wagoneer arrived in 1963, predating the Range Rover by seven years, and its wood-sided Grand Wagoneer finale became the Hamptons driveway default. Jeep revived the name in 2022 as a three-row flagship.
photoCredit: Photo: Sicnag, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Tesla
blurb: Forced the entire industry to go electric. The Model S proved EVs could be the fast option; the Model Y became the best-selling car in the world, of any kind.

name: Roadster
intro: The car that started it. Tesla's first product took a Lotus Elise chassis, replaced the running gear with batteries and a single electric motor, and proved in 2008 that an electric car could be the fast one. A successor has been promised for years and has not reached production.
photoCredit: Photo: Jeremy from Sydney, Australia, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Model S
intro: The car that forced every major maker to build an EV program. Launched in 2012 with range and acceleration no production EV had combined before, and still on sale, heavily revised underneath, more than a decade later.
photoCaption: 20180630 Tesla Model S 70D 2015 midnight blue left front
photoCredit: Photo: Granada, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Model 3
intro: Tesla's mass-market bet, and the car that took EVs mainstream: over two million sold, the best-selling EV in the world for stretches of its life, and the reason every legacy maker now has an electric sedan program.
photoCredit: Photo: AuHaidhausen, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Model Y
intro: The best-selling car in the world in 2023, not the best-selling EV, the best-selling car, full stop. The Model Y is the Model 3's formula raised onto a crossover body, and it outsells everything Tesla makes combined.
photoCaption: Tesla Model Y front passenger side view
photoCredit: Photo: Daniel.Cardenas, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Cybertruck
intro: Unveiled in 2019 with a smashed window on stage, delivered from late 2023. The Cybertruck's stainless wedge looks like a rendering error; underneath sit genuinely radical choices, steer-by-wire and a 48V architecture, wrapped in the most polarising truck ever sold.
photoCredit: Photo: A1C6, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: BMW
blurb: Started with aircraft engines, defined the sports sedan with the 3 Series, and built the M division into a byword for fast cars that still steer properly.

name: 3 Series
intro: The sports sedan benchmark for fifty years. Other brands build rivals; BMW builds the car they are measured against. The recipe has swollen and softened at times, but a straight-six 3 Series driven hard is still the reference.
photoCredit: Photo: Dinkun Chen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: 5 Series
intro: The executive sedan done the BMW way: rear-drive balance, a proper straight-six up front, and just enough aggression. At its best, the E39, it was possibly the finest sedan in the world.
photoCaption: BMW 5 SERIES LWB SEDAN (BMW G38) China
photoCredit: Photo: Dinkun Chen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: M3
intro: Born as a homologation special for touring-car racing, kept as the fast 3 Series with its own engine, chassis, and attitude. The market treats it as its own model, and so does everyone who has driven one.
photoCaption: BMW M3 (E30) Peter Brock Mobil race car
photoCredit: Photo: Yu Chu Chin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

intro: The car that saved BMW in America and invented the sports sedan formula: a boxy two-door, a willing four-cylinder, and handling that made contemporary Detroit iron feel broken. Every 3 Series since is an apology for, or a tribute to, this car.
photoCredit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

name: X5
intro: BMW insisted on calling it a Sports Activity Vehicle, and for once the marketing was honest: the X5 drove like a tall 5 Series when every rival drove like a truck. It built the performance-SUV segment the whole industry now lives in.
photoCredit: Photo: Vauxford, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Mercedes-Benz
blurb: Benz built the first automobile in 1886 and the company has been previewing the industry's future in the S-Class ever since. The 300SL is the collector benchmark.

name: S-Class
intro: The car the rest of the industry copies five years later. Air suspension, massaging seats, night vision, if it debuts anywhere, it debuts here. The name is short for Sonderklasse: special class. It has earned it more often than not.
photoCredit: Photo: Dinkun Chen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: E-Class
intro: The taxi in Stuttgart, the boardroom car everywhere else. The E-Class line, the W124 carried it before the name existed, is Mercedes at its most durable and least theatrical, which is exactly the point.
photoCredit: Photo: Dinkun Chen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: SL
intro: It starts with the 300SL Gullwing, the fastest production car of its day and still the collector benchmark, and continues as seven decades of open-top grand touring. The current car is an AMG product; the early car is automotive royalty.
photoCaption: 300 SL roadster, hood open, indoor show
photoCredit: Photo: Matti Blume, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: G-Class
intro: A military utility vehicle that became a luxury icon without changing its silhouette. Three locking differentials, a ladder frame, and door hinges on the outside, the shape is the substance, and Mercedes has wisely never messed with it.
photoCredit: Photo: MrWalkr, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: AMG GT
intro: AMG's own car, not a tuned Mercedes: a front-mid V8, a transaxle at the back, and a long bonnet with the cabin sitting nearly over the rear wheels. The second generation shares its bones with the SL and got more civilised; the first one is the purist's pick.
photoCaption: Dülmen, Automeile auf dem Kartoffelmarkt, Mercedes AMG GT -- 2019 -- 9884
photoCredit: Photo: Dietmar Rabich, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Porsche
blurb: One car, perfected for sixty years: the 911. Around it, Porsche built the most profitable sports-car company in the world without diluting the recipe.

intro: One car, perfected for sixty years. The engine is still in the wrong place, the silhouette is still a teardrop, and the 911 is still the sports car everything else is judged against, because Porsche never stopped developing it.
photoCaption: Porsche 911 Carrera S (991.2), the millionth 911, Irish Green, museum display
photoCredit: Photo: Matti Blume, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Cayenne
intro: The SUV that saved Porsche, purists hated it in 2002 and the profits funded every GT car since. It also happened to be genuinely good: fast, capable off-road, and unmistakably a Porsche to drive.
photoCredit: Photo: Alexander-93, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Taycan
intro: Porsche's first EV, built to answer one question: can an electric car feel like a Porsche? Two-speed rear gearbox, repeatable launch control, and steering that talks. The answer held up.
photoCredit: Photo: Evnerd, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

intro: The first production Porsche: a Beetle-derived aluminium coupe built in a sawmill in Gmünd, Austria, that became the template for everything after. Light, slippery, and quicker than cars with twice the power.
photoCredit: Photo: Berthold Werner, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: 718 Cayman/Boxster
intro: The Boxster saved Porsche in the 1990s; the Cayman coupe followed in 2005, and the pair became the handling benchmark money could buy. Renamed 718 in 2016 for the turbo flat-four era, then redeemed by the 4.0-litre sixes. Production of the petrol cars ended in 2025, with an electric successor planned.
photoCredit: Photo: Vauxford, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Volkswagen
blurb: The people's car, literally. The Beetle is one of the best-selling designs ever; the Golf GTI invented the hot hatch; the Bus became a cultural era on wheels.

name: Beetle
intro: The best-selling single design in car history, over 21 million originals. An air-cooled rear-engined economy car that outlived its century, then came back twice as nostalgia. The original is the one that matters.
photoCredit: Photo: Greg Gjerdingen, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Golf
intro: The Beetle's replacement and the car that defined the modern hatchback. The GTI variant invented the hot hatch in 1976, a family car with a big engine and red trim that embarrassed sports cars, and every generation since has had to live up to it.
photoCredit: Photo: Vauxford, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Type 2 (Bus)
intro: A delivery van that became a cultural era. The Bus carried hippies, surfboards, families, and half of Brazil, production there ran until 2013. Few vehicles have ever meant as much to as many different people.
photoCaption: Volkswagen Type 2 (T1) Samba, split-window bus, show field
photoCredit: Photo: Michael Barera, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Passat
intro: Volkswagen's sensible family car for fifty years, which produced some genuinely odd highlights, including a W8 engine nobody asked for. The US sedan ended in 2022, but the nameplate continues in Europe as a wagon and in China as a sedan.
photoCredit: Photo: Vauxford, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Audi
blurb: Quattro all-wheel drive changed rallying forever in 1980, then changed road cars. Audi sells technology and restraint in equal measure.

name: Quattro
intro: The original, Ur-Quattro in German, ur meaning ancestral. A turbocharged five-cylinder coupe with permanent all-wheel drive, launched in 1980 when that combination did not exist in a road car. It rewrote rallying, then rewrote what a fast road car was supposed to be. Every quattro-badged Audi since, the badge is lowercase for the system now, is this car's descendant.
photoCredit: Photo: Anna, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: A4
intro: Audi's 3 Series rival and the car that made its interiors the industry benchmark. The formula has been consistent for thirty years: restrained styling, a cabin a class above, and quattro all-wheel drive as the calling card.
photoCredit: Photo: Alexander-93, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: R8
intro: Audi's supercar, built on Lamborghini bones and better for being the sensible one: a V8, then a soaring naturally aspirated V10, behind the seats, all-wheel drive, and usability no Italian rival matched. The first generation's gated manual is already legend.
photoCredit: Photo: Hatsukari715, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

name: TT
intro: A design concept that escaped the motor show almost unchanged. The first TT was Bauhaus on wheels, a perfect geometric statement with a car underneath, and the line spent 25 years getting faster, peaking with the five-cylinder TT RS.
photoCredit: Photo: OSX, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Ferrari
blurb: A racing team that sells road cars to fund itself, and has never once pretended otherwise. V12s, scarlet paint, and waiting lists measured in years.

name: F40
intro: Enzo Ferrari's last signed-off car, built for the company's 40th anniversary. A twin-turbo V8, a Kevlar-and-carbon body, no ABS, no power steering, no apology. About 1,300 were built and it remains the rawest road car Ferrari has ever sold.
photoCredit: Photo: TTTNIS, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: LaFerrari
intro: Ferrari's hybrid flagship and its answer to the McLaren P1 and Porsche 918. A 6.3-litre V12 plus a KERS electric motor, 499 coupes, then 210 Aperta roadsters. Offered by invitation only, and most never left collections.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Testarossa
intro: The poster car of the 1980s. Side strakes feeding side-mounted radiators, a flat-12 mounted low in the middle, and a starring role on Miami Vice. Nearly 10,000 were built across the Testarossa, 512 TR and F512 M, huge numbers for a Ferrari flagship.
photoCredit: Photo: Mr.choppers, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Enzo
intro: Named for the founder and built as a Formula 1 car in road clothes, carbon tub, automated-manual gearbox, carbon-ceramic brakes, and aero that generated serious downforce without a big rear wing. 400 built, including the last one for the Pope.
photoCredit: Photo: TTTNIS, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Roma
intro: Ferrari's front-engined coupé in its softest suit: clean, retro-leaning styling, a 2+ cabin and the twin-turbo V8 from the Portofino turned up. The Spider convertible followed. It's the Ferrari for people who found the rest of the range too shouty.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Lamborghini
blurb: Ferruccio built tractors, got insulted by Enzo Ferrari, and answered with the Miura. Lamborghini has been the loud answer ever since, Countach posters defined a generation's bedroom walls.

name: Miura
intro: The car that invented the mid-engined supercar. Ferruccio Lamborghini's young engineers built it after hours, against his wishes, he wanted a grand tourer. The transverse V12 layout rewrote the rulebook permanently, and Gandini's styling has never been bettered at Sant'Agata.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Countach
intro: The wedge. Gandini's scissor-doored V12 spent sixteen years as the definitive poster car, growing wider, wingier and faster the whole way. Impractical, cramped, nearly impossible to reverse, and completely untouchable as an object.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Huracán
intro: The Gallardo's successor and the last of the naturally aspirated V10s. Over two decades of production variants, Evo, Performante, STO, Tecnica, Sterrato, made it Lamborghini's best-selling sports car before the Temerario replaced it in 2024.
photoCredit: Photo: Jakub Hałun, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Aventador
intro: The V12 flagship for a decade: carbon monocoque, pushrod suspension, scissor doors, and a 6.5-litre V12 that outlived three generations of rivals. Replaced by the hybrid Revuelto, which makes the Aventador the last pure-V12 Lamborghini flagship.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Urus
intro: The 'Super SUV' that doubled Lamborghini's sales and paid for everything else in the catalogue. Purists scoffed in 2018; the order books answered. Genuinely fast, genuinely usable, and the reason Lamborghini can still afford V12 flagships.
photoCredit: Photo: Alexander Migl, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Volvo
blurb: Gave the world the three-point seat belt and refused to patent it. Boxy wagons became a design language; the 240 simply refuses to die.

intro: The brick. Nearly three million built over nineteen years, and a significant number are still running, the 240 is the car that made Volvo's safety-and-durability reputation permanent. Slow, upright, honest, and close to immortal when maintained.
photoCredit: Photo: Rudolf Stricker, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: XC90
intro: Volvo's bestseller and the car that proved a seven-seat SUV could be about safety instead of size. The second-generation car's interior, open-pore wood, a portrait touchscreen, seats like armchairs, embarrassed German rivals at launch.
photoCredit: Photo: Vauxford, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: P1800
intro: Volvo's beautiful mistake: a curvaceous Italian-styled GT from a company known for boxes, built first by Jensen in England. Roger Moore drove one in The Saint, and one New York owner's car passed three million miles, the highest mileage ever recorded.
photoCredit: Photo: Berthold Werner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: V60
intro: The modern Volvo wagon done properly: long roof, low stance, and in T8 Polestar Engineered form, 455 hp nobody asked for and everybody wants. America's wagon drought made it a cult car here; in Sweden it was just a car.
photoCaption: Volvo V60 Polestar 2016 left front view
photoCredit: Photo: ITakePhotosOfCars, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Jaguar
blurb: The E-Type was called the most beautiful car ever made by Enzo Ferrari himself. Jaguar's history swings between genius and chaos, usually in the same decade.

name: E-Type
intro: Enzo Ferrari reportedly called it the most beautiful car ever made, and he was not wrong. 150 mph for a third of an Aston's price in 1961, on a monocoque with the XK engine and independent rear suspension. The standard every GT since has been judged against.
photoCredit: Photo: Berthold Werner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: XJ
intro: Jaguar's flagship saloon for half a century, from William Lyons' Series I to Ian Callum's radical X351. The XJ was always the driver's luxury car, lighter, lower and keener than the German default, when it wasn't being let down by 1970s build quality.
photoCredit: Photo: IFCAR, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

name: F-Type
intro: The E-Type's self-appointed heir: an aluminium two-seater with supercharged V6 and V8 engines and a crackling exhaust that became its signature. The facelift cleaned up the styling; the SVR turned it into a genuine supercar-baiter.
photoCredit: Photo: Ank Kumar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: XK120
intro: A show car that escaped. Jaguar built the XK120 for the 1948 London Motor Show as a showcase for its new XK engine, took hundreds of orders, and had to put it into production. It defined the British sports car for a generation and launched Jaguar's Le Mans era.
photoCredit: Photo: MrWalkr, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Land Rover
blurb: The 1948 Series I was a stopgap built from war-surplus aluminium; it became the default vehicle of farms, armies, and expeditions on every continent.

name: Defender
intro: Seventy years of farm, army and expedition service made the original Defender a British institution, and about as comfortable as one. The 2020 replacement kept the name and the look, replaced the ladder frame and live axles with a monocoque, and sold in numbers the original never approached.
photoCredit: Photo: Yu Chu Chin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Range Rover
intro: The original luxury SUV, from 1970: coil springs, a V8, and a design so right that one sat in the Louvre. Every generation since has traded a little more mud-plugging honesty for a lot more polish, and the fifth is now a full-scale limousine that can still wade nearly a metre of water.
photoCaption: 1995 Land Rover Range Rover Vogue TDi 2.5 Front
photoCredit: Photo: Makizox, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Discovery
intro: The middle child done right: seven seats, real off-road hardware and a stepped roof you can spot a mile away. The Discovery has always been the Land Rover for families who actually leave tarmac, even if the fifth generation dresses like it doesn't.
photoCredit: Photo: Rudolf Stricker, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Lexus
blurb: Toyota spent a billion dollars and five years building a Mercedes-beater in secret, then launched it in 1989 to a stunned industry. The luxury arm has been the quiet benchmark ever since, and built the LFA just to prove it could.

name: LS
intro: The car that launched a marque. Toyota's secret Flagship One project produced a V8 saloon quieter and cheaper than a Mercedes S-Class, and German boardrooms have respected Lexus ever since.
photoCredit: Photo: Dinkun Chen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: LFA
intro: A decade in development, a carbon tub, and a Yamaha-co-developed V10 that revs to 9,000 rpm faster than an analogue tach could follow, so the dial went digital. 500 built, each at a loss.
photoCredit: Photo: 先従隗始, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: IS
intro: Lexus's answer to the 3 Series, sold in Japan as the Toyota Altezza, chronograph-style instruments, a jewel of a straight six, and later the V8 IS 500 as a parting gift to the segment.
photoCredit: Photo: Kevauto, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: RX
intro: The original luxury crossover, a car-based SUV before the industry had a name for it. The RX hybrid of 2005 also made electrification a luxury feature rather than a compromise.
photoCredit: Photo: Szeremeta, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: LC
intro: The LF-LC concept car made production almost unchanged, a V8 grand tourer with concept-car surfacing, a ten-speed automatic, and one of the great interiors of its decade.
photoCredit: Photo: Matti Blume, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Alfa Romeo
blurb: Founded in Milan in 1910, Alfa won the first two Formula 1 world championships and employed a young Enzo Ferrari. The cars have always been emotional purchases, the Giulia Quadrifoglio is the current argument.

name: Giulia
intro: Project Giorgio: Alfa poached Ferrari engineers, spent billions, and produced a rear-drive sedan whose Quadrifoglio variant, with a Ferrari-derived twin-turbo V6, reset the sports-sedan benchmark.
photoCredit: Photo: Alexander Migl, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Stelvio
intro: The Giulia's platform under an SUV body, named for the pass with 48 hairpins. The Quadrifoglio version held the Nürburgring SUV lap record on launch.
photoCredit: Photo: KGC626, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Spider
intro: The Duetto: Pininfarina's round-tail roadster, Dustin Hoffman's co-star in The Graduate, and one of the longest-lived sports car designs ever, 28 years with the same basic body.
photoCredit: Photo: Ermell, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: 8C Competizione
intro: A concept car Alfa actually built: carbon body over a Maserati-derived chassis with Ferrari's 4.7 V8 up front. 500 coupés, then 500 Spiders, all sold before production began.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Giulia Sprint GT
intro: Bertone's stepped-nose coupé, styled by a young Giorgetto Giugiaro. The GTA variant, aluminium skin, twin-plug head, owned European touring car racing in the late 1960s.
photoCaption: Alfa Romeo Giulia Sprint GT family coupe, white, front 3/4
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Aston Martin
blurb: Lionel Martin raced specials at Aston Clinton hill climb; the company he founded in 1913 has gone bankrupt seven times and never stopped making the definitive British GT. Bond's DB5 made it immortal.

name: DB5
intro: The Goldfinger car, though the DB4 did the engineering, the DB5 did the immortality. Tadek Marek's twin-cam six, a ZF five-speed, and the template for every Aston since.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: V8 Vantage
intro: The Gaydon-era entry Aston: hand-assembled Jaguar-derived V8, a proper manual gearbox for most of its life, and styling that aged better than anything else in its class.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: DB11
intro: The first car of Aston's 'second century' plan: new bonded structure, a twin-turbo V12 of Aston's own, then an AMG V8 that many testers preferred for its lighter nose.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: DBX
intro: The SUV that saved Aston Martin, built in a new Welsh factory. The DBX707 briefly held the title of most powerful production SUV in the world.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Valkyrie
intro: Adrian Newey's road car: a Cosworth V12 revving to 11,000 rpm, a hybrid system filling the torque gaps, and downforce figures from a Formula 1 wind tunnel. 150 coupés, all spoken for.
photoCredit: Photo: Vauxford, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Cadillac
blurb: Henry Leland built Cadillac on interchangeable parts and precision machining in 1902. It defined American luxury for a century, tailfins, the Escalade, and a Blackwing line that out-handles the Germans.

name: Eldorado
intro: Fifty years of America's idea of luxury, from the hand-built 1953 convertible through the tallest tailfins ever fitted to a production car, to the final front-drive coupé of 2002.
photoCredit: Photo: Oleg Yunakov, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Escalade
intro: A Yukon Denali in a tuxedo that became a cultural fixture, and Cadillac's profit engine. The current car added a 38-inch curved OLED and a 682 hp V-Series.
photoCredit: Photo: Baron Maddock, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: CTS-V
intro: Corvette engines in a Cadillac sedan, three generations running. The second-gen wagon with a manual gearbox is one of the most collectible American cars of the 2010s.
photoCaption: 2009 Cadillac CTS-V in Black, front left (08-25-2009)
photoCredit: Photo: IFCAR, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

name: CT5-V Blackwing
intro: The last of its kind: a supercharged V8, rear-wheel drive, and a six-speed manual with no-lift shift, in a segment that went hybrid and all-wheel drive. Cadillac kept it in production because demand refused to die.
photoCredit: Photo: Damian B Oh, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Dodge
blurb: The Dodge brothers started as machinists supplying Ford before building their own car in 1914. The modern brand distilled itself to one idea, horsepower, cheap, and the Hellcat era was its glorious peak.

name: Charger
intro: From the 1968 car that defined the muscle silhouette, through two decades as a four-door sedan with Hellcat power, to the electric-and-six-cylinder Charger of 2024, the nameplate keeps reinventing the same idea.
photoCredit: Photo: Ermell, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Challenger
intro: Late to the pony-car fight in 1970, gone by 1974, then reborn in 2008 as a full-size retro coupé that outlived its rivals, and ended with the 840 hp Demon and the 1,025 hp Demon 170.
photoCaption: White Dodge Challenger SRT side view
photoCredit: Photo: Renée Kools, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Viper
intro: A V10, a tube frame, and no apology: no ABS, no traction control, no side windows on the first cars. Five generations of America's most honest sports car.
photoCaption: Dodge Viper RT/10 roadster, hood open, street
photoCredit: Photo: ArildV, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Durango
intro: Three rows and a Hemi for most of its life. The SRT Hellcat version, 710 hp, briefly the most powerful production SUV in the world, turned the school run into a drag strip.
photoCredit: Photo: Rutger van der Maar, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: GMC
blurb: GM's truck-only division since 1911. GMC sells the same bones as Chevrolet trucks with a premium brief, Denali became a luxury brand inside the brand, and the Hummer EV gave it an electric halo.

name: Sierra 1500
intro: Chevrolet's Silverado with a premium brief, and in Denali form, the truck that taught American luxury buyers to shop at a GMC store. C/K pickups carried the lineage before the Sierra name took over.
photoCredit: Photo: Alexander Migl, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Yukon
intro: The Tahoe's plusher twin since 1992. Yukon Denali became so dominant that 'Denali' is effectively GMC's luxury sub-brand, and the current XL is a genuine Escalade alternative.
photoCaption: 2021 GMC Yukon Denali in Hunter Metallic, front left
photoCredit: Photo: Mr.choppers, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Hummer EV
intro: The Hummer name reborn as a 4-tonne electric flagship: three motors, 1,000 hp, four-wheel steering with CrabWalk, and an open-air roof. Absurd, deliberate, and a genuine halo.
photoCredit: Photo: UltraTech66, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Syclone
intro: A turbocharged, all-wheel-drive S-10 that out-accelerated a Ferrari 348 in a famous 1991 comparison test. 2,995 built, all black, and the original American sport truck.
photoCaption: 1991 GMC Syclone in Black, front right (Saratoga)
photoCredit: Photo: Mr.choppers, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Kia
blurb: Korea's oldest carmaker spent decades as the budget option, then hired Peter Schreyer from Audi in 2006 and redesigned everything. The Stinger, Telluride, and EV6 are what the turnaround produced.

name: Stinger
intro: Kia's gran turismo: rear-drive, a twin-turbo V6, and chassis tuning by BMW M's former engineering chief Albert Biermann. It never sold like a 4 Series, which is why the good ones are bargains.
photoCredit: Photo: Ki hoon, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: EV6
intro: The E-GMP skateboard in a shooting-brake suit: 800-volt charging, a European Car of the Year trophy, and a GT flagship with 576 hp that embarrassed supercars at drag strips.
photoCredit: Photo: Alexander Migl, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Telluride
intro: The three-row that swept the 2020 awards, World Car of the Year, MotorTrend SUV of the Year, North American Utility of the Year, by being honest, handsome, and priced under the Germans it out-finished.
photoCredit: Photo: Gold Pony, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Soul
intro: The box the hamsters sold: a tall hatchback with genuine design wit that became Kia's American breakthrough car. Three generations over 16 years before the market moved to crossovers proper.
photoCredit: Photo: DieselFordMondeo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Lotus
blurb: Colin Chapman's doctrine, simplify, then add lightness, won seven Formula 1 constructors' titles and defined the British sports car. Now Geely-owned and electric-bound, with the Emira as the last petrol farewell.

name: Elan
intro: The definitive Chapman road car: a steel backbone chassis, fibreglass body, twin-cam power, and 675 kg. The Elan's steering feel is still the reference other roadsters are measured against, Mazda benchmarked it for the MX-5.
photoCaption: Lotus Elan S4 drop head coupe (front flank)
photoCredit: Photo: Grenadille, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Esprit
intro: Giugiaro's wedge, Bond's submarine, and 28 years of evolution from a 160 hp four to a twin-turbo V8. The last hand-built Lotus flagship and a study in keeping one design alive.
photoCredit: Photo: Corvesprit, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Elise
intro: The car that saved Lotus, named for Romano Artioli's granddaughter. A bonded aluminium tub at 725 kg proved in 1996 that lightness, not power, was the way back.
photoCredit: Photo: Thierry & Didier Descouens, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Emira
intro: The last petrol Lotus: AMG's turbo four or Toyota's supercharged V6, hydraulic steering feel, and supercar surfacing at sports-car money. A farewell written with unusual care.
photoCredit: Photo: MrWalkr, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Evija
intro: Lotus's electric reset: four motors, a 2,000 PS target, and Venturi tunnels through the rear bodywork. Eight customer cars a year make it the rarest thing Hethel has built.
photoCredit: Photo: Liam Walker, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Maserati
blurb: Six brothers from Bologna, a trident borrowed from a Neptune statue, and a century of racing and grand touring. Maserati has lived under Citroën, De Tomaso, Ferrari, and now Stellantis, the cars kept their opera regardless.

name: Ghibli (AM115)
intro: Giugiaro's masterpiece for Ghia: a long-bonnet GT with a quad-cam V8 and the longest, lowest silhouette of its era. The SS with the 4.9 is the one that matters.
photoCredit: Photo: 先従隗始, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Ghibli (M157)
intro: The modern Ghibli took the fight to the 5 Series with Ferrari-built twin-turbo engines and proper Italian drama. The Trofeo's 580 hp V8 made it a Q-car of the first order.
photoCredit: Photo: Navigator84, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Quattroporte
intro: The original sports saloon: Maserati put racing V8s in four-door bodies in 1963 and kept the nameplate alive for six generations until 2024.
photoCredit: Photo: Vauxford, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: GranTurismo
intro: Pininfarina's long-lived GT defined Maserati for a decade with a Ferrari V8; the second generation returned in 2023 with the Nettuno V6 and an all-electric Folgore flagship.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: MC12
intro: Maserati's return to racing, built on the Enzo's bones to homologate a GT1 car. Bigger, rarer, and in race trim far more successful than the Ferrari it came from, five FIA GT titles.
photoCredit: Photo: MrWalkr, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: MC20
intro: The Trident's clean-sheet supercar: a carbon tub, butterfly doors, and the Nettuno V6 with F1-style pre-chamber ignition, Maserati's own engine again, at last.
photoCredit: Photo: MrWalkr, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: McLaren
blurb: Bruce McLaren founded his race team in 1963; the road-car arm's first effort, the 1992 F1, is still the fastest naturally aspirated production car ever made. Everything since chases that standard in carbon fibre.

name: F1
intro: Gordon Murray's manifesto: a BMW V12, a carbon monocoque, a central driving seat, gold foil in the engine bay, and no turbos, no four-wheel drive, no compromise. Still the fastest naturally aspirated production car ever built.
photoCaption: McLaren F1 GT longtail road car, rear view
photoCredit: Photo: Ank Kumar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: P1
intro: The hybrid holy-trinity car from Woking: a twin-turbo V8 plus an electric motor filling every torque gap, active aero, and a Race mode that drops the car 50 mm. 375 built.
photoCredit: Photo: MrWalkr, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: 720S
intro: The second-generation Super Series car that humiliated everything at the drag strip: lighter, faster, and more usable than the class it redefined. Replaced by the 750S.
photoCredit: Photo: Y.Leclercq, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Senna
intro: Named for Ayrton, built for lap time: 800 kg of downforce, a door you can see the road through, and styling dictated entirely by the wind. 500 cars, all sold before the reveal.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Artura
intro: McLaren's reset: an all-new carbon architecture, a 120-degree V6 hybrid, and the electric-only running a supercar needs for the 2020s. The Spider is the pick of the range.
photoCaption: McLaren Artura MSO in purple (front view) at Japan Mobility Show Kansai 2025
photoCredit: Photo: Aos.1905, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: DeLorean
blurb: John Z. DeLorean left GM to build the car of the future: unpainted stainless panels, gullwing doors, and a factory in Dunmurry, Northern Ireland. One model, three model years, receivership in 1982, and, thanks to a time machine in a 1985 film, immortality.

name: DMC-12
intro: The only DeLorean: a Giugiaro wedge in brushed stainless steel over a Lotus-engineered backbone chassis, built in Northern Ireland with British government money. Underpowered, over budget, and, after Back to the Future, the most recognisable car of the 1980s.
photoCredit: Photo: Berthold Werner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Duesenberg
blurb: Fred and August Duesenberg built racing engines good enough to win Indianapolis and Le Mans outright; under E.L. Cord from 1926 they built the Model J, the grandest American car of its age, sold as a bare chassis to coachbuilders. The marque died with the Cord empire in 1937. The cars never did.

name: Model A
intro: The Duesenberg brothers' first production car, and a technical landmark: a straight-eight with an overhead cam in an era of flatheads, and four-wheel hydraulic brakes when rivals braked the rear wheels only.
photoCaption: 1921 Duesenberg Model A by Bender Body, front right, Greenwich 2021
photoCredit: Photo: Mr.choppers, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Model J
intro: Unveiled at the 1928 New York show as a chassis alone costing more than a whole Cadillac: 265 hp when 100 was a lot, built to carry the greatest coachwork of the age, Murphy, LeBaron, Derham, Figoni. The definitive American classic.
photoCredit: Photo: Michael Barera, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Packard
blurb: 'Ask the man who owns one.' Founded in Warren, Ohio and Detroit-based from 1903, Packard was American luxury's default answer for half a century, Twin Sixes, straight-eights and Twelves built to the standard Rolls-Royce was measured against. A merger with Studebaker and a changing market ended it in 1958; the best Packards remain blue-chip classics.

name: Twelve
intro: Packard's V12 flagship, launched as the Twin Six in 1932, renamed Twelve a year later, was Detroit's answer to the great European chassis: silent, torquey, and bodied by the best shops in America.
photoCredit: Photo: Valder137, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Super Eight
intro: The straight-eight backbone of the Packard range for nearly two decades, the car most people meant by 'a Packard', spanning the Classic era, the streamline years and the first postwar cars.
photoCaption: 1938 Packard Super Eight Club Sedan, front left (2022 Portersville Summer Steam Show)
photoCredit: Photo: MercurySable99, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Caribbean
intro: Packard's halo car of the fifties: a low-volume convertible with continental flair, wire wheels and tri-tone paint, built to fight Cadillac's Eldorado. The 1956 hardtop joined for the final year.
photoCredit: Photo: Oleg Yunakov, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Hawk
intro: The last real Packard, built for one year on Studebaker bones in South Bend: a supercharged Golden Hawk in Packard dress, with padded armrests on the outside of the doors and the marque's final flourish of fins.
photoCredit: Photo: GPS 56 from New Zealand, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Saab
blurb: An aircraft company that built cars like aircraft: teardrop bodies, two-stroke engines, front-wheel drive proven in Swedish snow, and turbocharging for everyone years before it was fashion. GM ownership ended in the 2011 bankruptcy; the faithful, and the cars, never really left.

intro: Saab's first three decades in one line: a teardrop two-stroke shaped by aircraft engineers, evolved from the 92 through the 93 to the long-lived 96, rally winner, family staple, and the car that made front-wheel drive make sense in winter.
photoCredit: Photo: Lukasz19930915, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

intro: The bigger, safer Saab: wraparound windscreen, ignition by the handbrake, and in 1978 the 99 Turbo, one of the first production cars to make turbocharging a road-car virtue rather than a racing trick.
photoCredit: Photo: Liftarn, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

intro: The Saab most people picture: the upright windscreen, the deep hatch, the turbo whistle. The 'classic' 900 ran fifteen years and made the marque; its GM-platform successor shared the name and little else.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

intro: Saab's big car, developed with Fiat, Lancia and Alfa Romeo on the shared Type Four programme, but characteristically Saabified, and in Aero form one of the great sleepers: mid-range punch that embarrassed period supercars.
photoCredit: Photo: Indie102, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

intro: The 900's successor under GM, twice over: first a deep facelift of the old car, Viggen included, then the 2003 Sport Sedan, all-new, with the Aero V6 and the all-wheel-drive Turbo X as its peaks. NEVS briefly restarted the line in 2013.
photoCredit: Photo: OSX, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

intro: The 9000's replacement and Saab's flagship for fifteen years: the thinking driver's E-Class alternative, with the Aero estate as the connoisseur's express. Its handsome 2010 successor arrived just in time for the bankruptcy, and production stayed tiny.
photoCredit: Photo: Rutger van der Maar, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Studebaker
blurb: Wagon-maker in 1852 and carmaker from 1902, Studebaker was America's great independent for six decades. Raymond Loewy's studio gave it the landmark 1953 coupes and the Avanti; the Lark nearly saved it. South Bend closed in 1963 and the last cars came from Canada in 1966, the designs aged better than the balance sheet.

name: Loewy Coupes (Starlight / Starliner)
intro: The 1953 coupes designed under Raymond Loewy, Robert Bourke's clean, low, European line, are regularly called the most beautiful American cars of the fifties. They became the foundation of the Hawk line that followed.
photoCaption: 1952 Studebaker Commander Starliner Hardtop Coupe - fvl (5446952891)
photoCredit: Photo: Rex Gray, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Lark
intro: The compact that saved Studebaker for a while: launched in 1959 just as America discovered small cars, it briefly returned the company to profit, and with the optional V8s, it was quietly quick.
photoCaption: 1959 Studebaker Lark VIII hardtop, front left, 08-27-2023
photoCredit: Photo: MercurySable99, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Gran Turismo Hawk
intro: Brooks Stevens restyled the Loewy coupe's bones into a formal, Mercedes-tinged GT for 1962, the last Studebaker with real money spent on it, and a credible grand tourer at a Chevrolet price.
photoCaption: 1962 Studebaker Gran Turismo Hawk, front left, 07-04-2025
photoCredit: Photo: MercurySable99, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Avanti
intro: Raymond Loewy's team designed it in weeks; Brooks Stevens' studio finished it: a fibreglass, bottom-breather GT with a supercharged option, roll bar built in, and speed records at Bonneville. Studebaker died; the Avanti, built by others, lived on for decades.
photoCredit: Photo: Michael Barera, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Tucker
blurb: Preston Tucker promised the car of tomorrow, today: rear-engined, a centre 'Cyclops Eye' headlight that steered with the wheels, and safety engineered in from the first sketch. Fifty-one cars were built before the company collapsed amid an SEC trial that ended in acquittal. The 48 is America's most famous almost.

intro: The 'Tin Goose' prototype and fifty production cars: a rear-engined, flat-six sedan years ahead of Detroit, padded dash, pop-out windscreen, a third headlight that turned with the steering, and a corporation that became a courtroom legend.
photoCaption: Tucker 48 sedan 1948, front 3/4, Gilmore Car Museum
photoCredit: Photo: Greg Gjerdingen, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: AMC
blurb: Born of the Nash–Hudson merger in 1954, American Motors survived by being cleverer than the giants: compacts when compacts weren't cool, the Javelin and AMX for the muscle years, and the Eagle, all-wheel drive for ordinary families, a generation before the crossover era. Chrysler absorbed AMC in 1987, mostly for Jeep.

name: Javelin
intro: AMC's pony car, and a good one: styled by Dick Teague, raced by Penske, and armed with engines up to the 401. The second-generation car won the Trans-Am championship outright in 1971 and 1972.
photoCredit: Photo: Xnatedawgx, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: AMX
intro: America's other two-seat sports car: a Javelin with a foot cut out of the wheelbase, a 390 V8 option, and a name made of the company's initials. Craig Breedlove took one to Bonneville records before it even went on sale.
photoCredit: Photo: Michael Barera, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Gremlin
intro: Introduced on April Fool's Day, 1970, a Rambler American with the back chopped off, styled on an air-sickness bag according to legend. Cheap, cheeky, and with the optional 304 V8, absurdly quick for a subcompact.
photoCredit: Photo: Captainpisslord, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Pacer
intro: The wide small car: as broad as a full-size sedan, glass everywhere, and one door longer than the other so rear passengers could climb in. Designed for a rotary engine GM cancelled, immortalised by Wayne's World.
photoCredit: Photo: CZmarlin, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Eagle
intro: The crossover, invented fifteen years early: a Concord body on full-time all-wheel drive with raised suspension, in wagon, sedan, coupe and the SX/4 hatch. Subaru and every modern crossover owe it a footnote at least.
photoCaption: 1981-1984 AMC Eagle 4-door sedan, front left view
photoCredit: Photo: MercurySable99, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Pontiac
blurb: GM's excitement division, by its own slogan and by the evidence: launched in 1926 as a companion to Oakland, it soon outsold its parent. The GTO started the muscle-car era in 1964, the Trans Am owned the late seventies, and the Solstice was a last flash of the old fire before GM closed the marque in 2010.

name: GTO
intro: The original muscle car: John DeLorean's team slipped a 389 big-block into a mid-size Tempest in 1964 and the era began. Judge, Ram Air, a wilderness decade, and a final Australian-built encore in 2004.
photoCredit: Photo: Greg Gjerdingen, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Firebird / Trans Am
intro: Pontiac's F-body, four generations deep: Ram Air originals, the SD-455, the Bandit phenomenon, Knight Rider, and a final LS1 WS6 that was a Corvette in a tuxedo t-shirt.
photoCaption: 1977 Pontiac Firebird Trans Am, front right, 06-21-2023
photoCredit: Photo: MercurySable99, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Grand Prix
intro: Pontiac's personal-luxury nameplate for 46 years: born as a full-size performance coupe with bucket seats and a 421 option, ending as a supercharged front-drive sedan, the GXP even got a V8.
photoCredit: Photo: MercurySable99, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Bonneville
intro: Named for the salt flats and launched as a fuel-injected convertible flagship in 1957, every first-year car was a convertible, and 'fuel injection' was Pontiac announcing it had arrived as a performance brand.
photoCaption: 1966 Pontiac Bonneville Convertible, front right (Cruisin' the River Lowellville Car Show, July 10th, 2023)
photoCredit: Photo: MercurySable99, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Fiero
intro: America's mid-engine commuter car that became a sports car just in time to be cancelled: plastic panels on a spaceframe, a V6 GT by 1985, and a proper fastback for 1986. The 1988 suspension, finally all Pontiac's own design, was the best and the last.
photoCredit: Photo: Mr.choppers, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Solstice
intro: Bob Lutz's back-to-basics roadster and Pontiac's last halo: a concept car (2002) willed into production, outselling the MX-5 in its first year, with the turbo GXP and a rare targa coupe as the collector endings.
photoCredit: Photo: MercurySable99, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Oldsmobile
blurb: Ransom E. Olds founded the marque in 1897 and the Curved Dash made it America's first high-volume carmaker. The Rocket 88 put a modern overhead-valve V8 in a light body in 1949, the Toronado pioneered modern front-wheel drive, and the 4-4-2 carried the muscle years. GM phased Oldsmobile out in 2004, 107 years young.

name: Curved Dash Oldsmobile
intro: The car that started mass production's story: a $650 single-cylinder runabout built in the thousands while rivals built dozens, the first Oldsmobile, and for a while the best-selling car in America.
photoCredit: Photo: Rutger van der Maar, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: 88 / Rocket 88
intro: The 1949 Rocket 88, a modern overhead-valve V8 in the lighter body, is a founding document of the muscle-car idea and the subject of what is often called the first rock-and-roll record. The 88 nameplate then ran for fifty years.
photoCredit: Photo: Alfvanbeem, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

intro: Four-barrel, four-speed, dual exhausts, the name was the spec sheet. Born as a police-package option in the GTO's shadow, the 4-4-2 became its own model and, in 455 W-30 form, one of the era's fastest.
photoCaption: 1967 Oldsmobile 442 hardtop coupe, hood open, show field
photoCredit: Photo: Michael Barera, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Toronado
intro: The car that brought front-wheel drive back to America: a 7-litre V8 driving the front wheels through a chain-driven transaxle, styled like a jet-age sculpture. It worked, it sold, and it changed GM's engineering map.
photoCredit: Photo: MercurySable99, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Cutlass
intro: For a time, the Cutlass was simply the best-selling car in America, the nameplate that carried Oldsmobile's volume from the muscle era through the G-body years, with the Supreme as the default upgrade buy of the suburbs.
photoCaption: 1985 Oldsmobile Cutlass Supreme sedan in Dark Chestnut Metallic, front left, 1-11-2021
photoCredit: Photo: BlueCrabRedCrab, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Aurora
intro: Oldsmobile's last flagship and its best car in decades: a Northstar-derived 4.0 V8, a rigid shell, and concept-car styling, the car that was meant to save the marque and instead became its elegant farewell.
photoCaption: 1996 Oldsmobile Aurora in Silver Teal (front left side)
photoCredit: Photo: Flybrian at English Wikipedia, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Plymouth
blurb: Chrysler's value brand, launched in 1928, with a performance streak a mile wide: the Barracuda beat the Mustang to market by two weeks in 1964, the Road Runner made speed cheap, and the Hemi 'Cuda became the muscle market's ceiling. The Voyager helped invent the minivan in 1984. Chrysler retired the marque in 2001.

name: Barracuda
intro: Launched April 1, 1964, two weeks before the Mustang, on Valiant bones with the biggest rear window in the business. By 1970 the E-body 'Cuda had become the muscle era's apex predator, and the Hemi convertible its holy grail.
photoCredit: Photo: Mustang Joe, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Road Runner
intro: Plymouth paid Warner Bros. for the cartoon bird and spent the savings on speed: a stripped B-body, a 383 with magnum internals, and a 'meep meep' horn. The 1970 Superbird wore a nose cone and a wing for NASCAR, and for immortality.
photoCredit: Photo: MercurySable99, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: GTX
intro: The gentleman's muscle car: Plymouth's upscale B-body with the 440 Super Commando standard and the Hemi on the option list, pitched at buyers who wanted the pace without the stripper spec.
photoCredit: Photo: Greg Gjerdingen from Willmar, USA, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Duster
intro: The budget bruiser: a Valiant fastback coupe that, with the 340 small-block, outran cars twice its price and embarrassed its own stablemates. The Twister trim sold the look; the 340 sold the legend.
photoCredit: Photo: Jeremy from Sydney, Australia, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Prowler
intro: A factory hot rod in 1997: aluminium-intensive, open-wheeled retro styling, and a concept car Chrysler actually built. The V6-only powertrain was the compromise; the look was not.
photoCredit: Photo: Greg Gjerdingen from Willmar, USA, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Voyager
intro: With the Dodge Caravan, the 1984 Voyager invented the modern minivan: front-wheel drive, a car floor height, and a sliding door, selling families out of station wagons by the millions. Lee Iacocca's second act saved Chrysler.
photoCaption: 1984-86 Plymouth Voyager LE in Garnet Red Pearl Coat, front right
photoCredit: Photo: Ethan Llamas, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Cord
blurb: E.L. Cord's own nameplate, built by Auburn: America's first front-wheel-drive production cars, and in the 810 a design so advanced the Museum of Modern Art put it on a pedestal. The empire fell in 1937. The cars never fell at all.

name: L-29
intro: The first American production car with front-wheel drive: E.L. Cord's answer to a market that thought drive belonged at the back. Low, long and handsome, it sold refinement and novelty in equal measure, until the Depression sold neither.
photoCredit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

intro: Gordon Buehrig's masterpiece and the most advanced American car of its decade: front-wheel drive, hidden headlamps, a supercharger option, and not one exposed hinge or running board. It arrived too late and too expensive to save the company, and became immortal anyway.
photoCaption: Cord 810/812 Westchester sedan, front 3/4, concours grass
photoCredit: Photo: David Berry, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Hudson
blurb: Detroit's cleverest independent: the step-down body of 1948 put passengers inside the frame rails and made Hudsons handle like nothing else in America, and the Hornet's big six beat the V8s at their own game on the NASCAR circuit. Merged into AMC in 1954; the name ended in 1957.

name: Essex
intro: Hudson's budget line that outsold its parent: the Essex made closed cars affordable, put a six-cylinder engine in reach of ordinary buyers, and carried Hudson through the 1920s. The Super Six name above it said everything about the formula, more cylinders, less money.
photoCredit: Photo: Тимба, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Terraplane
intro: Launched off the Essex County Airport runway in 1932, the name is the point, the Terraplane was Hudson's volume fighter: steel-bodied, quick for its price, and famous enough that bluesman Robert Johnson sang about one. It became simply 'Hudson' after 1938.
photoCredit: Photo: Joe Ross from Lansing, Michigan, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Jet
intro: Hudson's compact gamble: a small, tall, well-equipped sedan launched into the teeth of the horsepower war. It was a good car in the wrong year, and its development cost is part of why Hudson merged into AMC in 1954.
photoCaption: 1953 Hudson Super Jet 4-Door Sedan, front left (Cruisin' the River Lowellville Car Show, June 19th, 2023)
photoCredit: Photo: MercurySable99, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Hornet
intro: The step-down Hudson at its peak: a low, unit-body sedan whose big six humiliated V8s on the early NASCAR circuit, 'Fabulous Hudson Hornet' was a results sheet before it was a cartoon. The last true Hudsons before the AMC years turned it into a badge.
photoCaption: Hudson Hornet 1952 RSideRear Lake Mirror Cassic 16Oct2010 (14876876262)
photoCredit: Photo: Valder137, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Nash
blurb: Charles Nash built the industry's quiet innovator: overhead-valve engines, unit bodies, reclining seats, and in the 1950 Rambler, America's first successful compact. Nash merged with Hudson to form AMC in 1954, and its Rambler idea became the new company's whole future.

name: Ambassador
intro: Nash's flagship for a quarter century: overhead-valve engines when rivals ran flatheads, unit construction, reclining seats, and the bathtub Airflyte styling that defined post-war Nash. The nameplate outlived the company, AMC kept building Ambassadors after Nash itself was gone.
photoCredit: Photo: CZmarlin, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Rambler
intro: The car that started the American compact era: George Romney's bet that a smaller, cheaper, well-equipped Nash could beat the Big Three's bulk. It could. The Rambler name went on to anchor AMC, and this little Airflyte convertible is where it began.
photoCredit: Photo: Christopher Ziemnowicz, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Metropolitan
intro: An American idea built in England: Nash commissioned Austin to build its tiny Metropolitan in Birmingham, sold it as a Nash and then a Hudson, and proved a market for small cars existed a decade before Detroit admitted it. Two-tone paint and a continental spare were standard charm.
photoCredit: Photo: Greg Gjerdingen from Willmar, USA, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Nash-Healey
intro: America's first post-war sports car beat the Corvette to market: Donald Healey's chassis, Nash's overhead-valve six, and from 1952 a Pininfarina body built in Turin. A Nash-Healey finished third overall at Le Mans in 1952, the marque's finest hour, in a car almost nobody bought.
photoCredit: Photo: Vauxford, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Kaiser
blurb: Shipbuilder Henry J. Kaiser took on Detroit from the world's largest factory building, with partner Joseph Frazer: for one year, 1947, Kaiser-Frazer outsold every other independent. The cars were handsome, the six was honest, and the Big Three's scale won in the end. US car production ended in 1955.

name: Kaiser (Special / Deluxe / Manhattan)
intro: Henry J. Kaiser's post-war challenger: built in Ford's vast Willow Run plant, styled with real flair by 1951, and powered throughout by the same Continental six, which is why the Manhattan's 1954 supercharger mattered. Kaiser outsold every other independent in 1947 and never quite caught the Big Three again.
photoCredit: Photo: Stephen Foskett, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Henry J
intro: The $1,300 car: Kaiser's austerity special, named for the boss, built to undercut everyone. No trunk lid on early cars, you loaded through the folded seat. It sold respectably, seeded the compact idea at Kaiser, and survives today mostly as gasser drag-car raw material.
photoCredit: Photo: Hugo90, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Darrin
intro: The Kaiser-Darrin: a fibreglass sports car with doors that slide into the front wings, launched the same season as the Corvette and gone within the year. Howard 'Dutch' Darrin put his name on it; Kaiser built 435 before the money ran out.
photoCredit: Photo: MercurySable99, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Stutz
blurb: Harry Stutz debuted at Indianapolis in 1911 and finished eleventh with no mechanical trouble, 'the car that made good in a day.' The Bearcat made the marque; the Vertical Eight and the twin-cam DV-32 kept it at the luxury summit until 1937.

name: Bearcat
intro: The brass-age sports car in its purest form: two bucket seats, a fuel tank, a huge four-cylinder engine and nothing else. The Bearcat made Stutz's name at Indianapolis in 1911, 'the car that made good in a day', and the name returned on the supercharged DV-32 cars of the thirties.
photoCredit: Photo: Katherine Tompkins, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Vertical Eight (Safety Stutz)
intro: Stutz reinvented itself as a luxury marque: the Vertical Eight brought an overhead-cam straight-eight, hydraulic brakes and safety glass to a company built on speed, and the Weymann fabric-body cars gave it Parisian style. The Blackhawk speed records of 1928 were the proof of speed.
photoCaption: 1928 Stutz Blackhawk boattail speedster, museum display
photoCredit: Photo: Alan Raine, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Triumph
blurb: A bicycle company that became Britain's sports-car export champion: the TR line sold the open two-seater to America for three decades, the Stag aimed at Mercedes, and the Dolomite Sprint quietly invented the mass-produced sixteen-valve engine. Car production ended in 1984; the name survives with BMW.

name: TR2 / TR3
intro: The post-war British sports car distilled: a twin-carburettor twin-seater with cut-down doors, a 100 mph top speed and a price Detroit couldn't touch. The TR line started here, and so did a generation of American sports-car racing.
photoCredit: Photo: Daniel Milner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: TR4 / TR5 / TR250
intro: Michelotti civilised the TR: wind-up windows, a proper boot, and an optional Surrey top, then the TR5 added fuel injection and six cylinders' worth of pace. America got carburettors and the TR250 name instead, which is why the injected cars are the legend.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: TR6
intro: Karmann sharpened the TR5's suit and Triumph kept the recipe: a big six, a separate chassis, and 150,000 buyers, nearly all of them American. The last of the traditional hairy-chested TRs before the wedge arrived.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: TR7 / TR8
intro: 'The shape of things to come': Harris Mann's wedge replaced a decade of tradition with pop-up lamps and a fixed head, and the launch quality troubles wrote the headlines. The TR8's Rover V8 fixed the pace problem just as production ended, which is why it is the one everyone wants now.
photoCredit: Photo: Vauxford, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Spitfire
intro: Michelotti's small sports car on Herald bones: a flip-forward bonnet, swing axles with opinions, and 315,000 buyers over eighteen years. The Spitfire was the sports car students could afford and the one half the paddock started in.
photoCaption: White Triumph Spitfire Mk3 with hardtop - side
photoCredit: Photo: Akela NDE, CC BY-SA 2.0 fr, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Stag
intro: Triumph's grand idea: a four-seat convertible with a home-grown 3.0 V8, a T-bar roof and Michelotti styling aimed squarely at Mercedes' SL. The engine's cooling troubles wrote its reputation; the survivors, mostly cured by forty years of club knowledge, are the grand tourers the car always meant to be.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Dolomite
intro: The Sprint is the headline: a 2.0-litre sixteen-valve head, the first mass-produced multi-valve engine, on a Michelotti sedan that embarrassed bigger cars in touring-car racing. The ordinary Dolomites were worthy family cars; the Sprint was a factory hot rod in a cardigan.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Austin-Healey
blurb: Born in a single evening at the 1952 Earls Court show: Donald Healey's sports car, Austin's engines and factories. The Big Healeys ruled early-sixties rallying, the Frogeye Sprite put a smile on the cheapest sports car in Britain, and the badge partnership ended in 1971.

intro: The Healey 100 that Austin built: Donald Healey's Earls Court show car of 1952, adopted by Leonard Lord overnight and put into production at Longbridge with Austin's big four. A hundred miles an hour for a thousand pounds, the name is the spec sheet.
photoCredit: Photo: Peter & Laila, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

intro: The six-cylinder Healey: BMC's C-series engine replaced the four, the wheelbase stretched for occasional rear seats, and the car grew from sports car toward grand tourer. The 1958 cars, built at Abingdon alongside the MGs, are the sweet spot of the line.
photoCredit: Photo: Pierre,Sami & Roxi Cola, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

intro: The Big Healey at full size: 2.9 litres, disc brakes, and a rally record, Pat Moss, the Morley brothers, wins at the Liège and the Alpine, that made it the definitive British competition car of the sixties. The Mk III's wood dash and wind-up windows civilised it without softening it.
photoCaption: Austin-Healey 3000 Mk II BN7 (1962) Solitude Revival 2022 1X7A0090
photoCredit: Photo: Alexander Migl, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Sprite
intro: The Frogeye: a Healey sports car for £669, its headlamps perched on the bonnet because the flip-up mechanism cost too much. The Sprite democratised the sports car a second time and raced everywhere; its MG Midget twin kept the shape alive to 1979.
photoCredit: Photo: MrWalkr, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Jensen
blurb: The Jensen brothers' West Bromwich works built bodies for half the industry, then their own cars: fibreglass GTs first, then the Interceptor, Italian styling, American V8, and in the FF the world's first four-wheel-drive, anti-lock-braked production car. Production ended in 1976.

intro: Jensen's fibreglass pioneer: a glass-bodied GT with Austin's four-litre six, a Perspex rear window and a drag figure that embarrassed steel cars. The 541R added disc brakes all round, a British first on a production four-seater, and the 541S finished the line in comfort.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: C-V8
intro: Before the Interceptor, the formula: Chrysler V8 power in a West Bromwich fibreglass body, with the canted quad headlamps that half the press hated and the other half never forgot. One of the fastest four-seaters of its day, full stop.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Interceptor
intro: The definitive Jensen: Touring of Milan's steel body, that vast curved rear window, Chrysler V8 torque, and in the FF, four-wheel drive and anti-lock brakes years before Audi made the quattro famous. It was the car rock stars bought instead of an Aston, and it has never stopped looking like money.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Jensen-Healey
