intro: Jensen's bid for the American sports-car market after the Big Healey ended: Donald Healey's name, a Lotus twin-cam engine, and styling built for California. Engine teething troubles hurt it early; sorted cars are the quick, comfortable classic the spec sheet always promised.
photoCredit: Photo: ozzadavies, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: TVR
blurb: Trevor Wilkinson started TVR in a Blackpool wheelwright's shop; under Peter Wheeler it became British sports-car making at its most gloriously uncompromising, glassfibre bodies, backbone chassis, enormous power-to-weight and a standing refusal of driver aids. The factory closed in 2006.

name: Grantura
intro: The first production TVR: a glassfibre coupé on a backbone chassis, sold with whatever engine the decade offered, Climax, Ford, BMC, MG. Light, stark and quick, it set the template every TVR since has followed: minimum weight, maximum engine, no apologies.
photoCaption: 1961 TVR Grantura Mark IIA, front left (Hershey 2019)
photoCredit: Photo: Mr.choppers, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Griffith
intro: Two cars, one idea, thirty years apart. Jack Griffith stuffed a Ford 289 into a Grantura in New York and built America's Cobra rival; Peter Wheeler stuffed Rover's V8 into a nineties roadster and built Britain's. Both are light, loud and entirely serious about power-to-weight.
photoCredit: Photo: SG2012, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Chimaera
intro: TVR's best-seller: the Griffith's running gear in a softer, roomier roadster that sold over 6,000 copies and kept Blackpool busy for a decade. It is the usable TVR, which in TVR terms still means a Rover V8, a glassfibre body and no safety net.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Cerbera
intro: The 2+2 that took TVR racing: Peter Wheeler's brief was a Porsche 911 rival with TVR's own engines, the flat-plane AJP8 V8 and the Speed Six, designed in-house because Rover power wasn't enough anymore. The Cerbera Speed 12, its unhinged sibling, never reached customers. This one did, barely tamed.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Tuscan
intro: The Speed Six engine in a body with a removable roof panel, no door handles and curves that owed nothing to a wind tunnel. The Tuscan was TVR's millennium flagship, the car from Swordfish, and the last of the Wheeler-era volume models.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Sagaris
intro: The last Wheeler TVR and the most extreme: a Tuscan underneath, endurance-racer vents cut into every panel, a clear rear spoiler and a 400 hp Speed Six. Built for two years before the factory closed; it reads now as the marque's full stop, exclamation included.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Austin
blurb: Herbert Austin built the Seven that motorised Britain, then the Longbridge works carried the Mini, the 1100 and the Metro, the cars ordinary Britain actually drove. The marque faded through the BMC and British Leyland years and was retired in the late 1980s.

name: Seven
intro: The car that motorised Britain. Herbert Austin's baby car put a real automobile, four cylinders, four wheels, brakes all round eventually, within reach of families who had managed with a motorcycle and sidecar, and licensed production spread the design from Munich (the first BMW) to Tokyo and New York.
photoCredit: Photo: DeFacto, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: A30 / A35
intro: Austin's first post-war small car and the A-series engine's debut. The A35 of 1956 sharpened it with the 948 cc engine, and A35s became unlikely giant-killers in saloon-car racing, they still race at Goodwood today, sideways and entirely serious.
photoCredit: Photo: Andrew Bone from Weymouth, England, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Mini
intro: Alec Issigonis's transverse-engine, front-drive rethink of the small car: ten feet long, room for four, and a layout the whole industry eventually copied. Sold as an Austin (Seven, then Mini) and a Morris, it won Monte Carlo rallies, carried the sixties, and stayed in production for 41 years.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: 1100 / 1300 (ADO16)
intro: Britain's best-selling car of the sixties: Issigonis's larger car, with Hydrolastic suspension, front-wheel drive and Pininfarina-influenced lines. Badged as Austin, Morris, MG, Riley, Vanden Plas and Wolseley, the 1300 GT and the MG 1300 are the sporting faces of the range.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Metro
intro: The 'British car to beat the world', launched to replace the Mini and instead sold alongside it for seventeen years. The MG Metro and the turbocharged MG Metro Turbo carried the sporting brief; the late Rover-badged cars (from 1990, as the Rover 100) gained the K-series engine.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Borgward
blurb: Carl F. W. Borgward built Germany's most inventive post-war car group, the first new German design of 1949, the Isabella, air suspension on the P100, then lost it all in the sudden, still-argued collapse of 1961.

name: Hansa 1500 / 1800
intro: The first new German car design after the war: a ponton-bodied saloon from Carl Borgward's Bremen works, shown at Geneva in 1949 when most rivals were still selling pre-war shapes. The Hansa name came from Borgward's pre-war marque.
photoCredit: Photo: User Spurzem on de.wikipedia, CC BY-SA 2.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Isabella
intro: Borgward's masterpiece and its best-seller: a clean-lined monocoque saloon named, the story goes, because Carl Borgward told his staff to write 'Isabella' on the test reports so rivals would not know what was coming. The coupé is one of the prettiest German cars of the fifties.
photoCredit: Photo: Lothar Spurzem, CC BY-SA 2.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Arabella
intro: The small Borgward, built to take the group downmarket against the Beetle and the Kadett, a water-cooled flat-four (a rarity then and now) in a neat two-door saloon. It arrived just as the money ran out, and barely 47,000 were built.
photoCredit: Photo: Charles from Port Chester, New York, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: P100
intro: Borgward's flagship and Germany's first production car with air suspension: a 2.3-litre six in a formal ponton body, aimed squarely at Mercedes. Fewer than 2,600 were built before the 1961 collapse, making it the rarest route into the marque's top drawer.
photoCredit: Photo: Charles01, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: De Tomaso
blurb: Alejandro de Tomaso, an Argentine racer settled in Modena, built the formula that defined the marque for thirty years: Italian design, a mid-mounted Ford V8, and American dealer reach. The Pantera sold from 1971 to 1992.

name: Vallelunga
intro: Alejandro de Tomaso's first road car: a mid-engined coupé with a backbone chassis, Ford Cortina power and Ghia or Fissore bodywork. Only about 58 were built, but the layout, mid-engine, Italian body, Ford engine, became the De Tomaso formula for thirty years.
photoCredit: Photo: Andrew Bone from Weymouth, England, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Mangusta
intro: The mongoose, the animal that kills cobras, drawn by Giorgetto Giugiaro at Ghia around a backbone chassis and a Ford V8. Gullwing covers over the engine, a split rear deck, and proportions that still stop traffic. About 400 were built.
photoCredit: Photo: Valder137, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Pantera
intro: The De Tomaso that conquered America: Tom Tjaarda's wedge, a Ford 351 Cleveland amidships, sold through Lincoln-Mercury dealers with a Ford warranty. Group 4 racers, the wide-body GT5 cars of the eighties, and the final Si, the Pantera outlived its maker-era rivals by two decades.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Longchamp
intro: De Tomaso's front-engined luxury coupé, Tjaarda again, Ford Cleveland power, and a chassis shared with the Deauville saloon and the Maserati Kyalami. About 409 coupés were built across a long, quiet production life, plus a handful of Spyder convertibles.
photoCaption: De Tomaso Longchamp Gen1 000 1973-1979 frontleft 2011-04-17 A
photoCredit: Photo: Detectandpreserve, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Guarà
intro: The last De Tomaso: a carbon-kevlar and aluminium sports car with pushrod suspension, launched with BMW V8 power and finished, after Alejandro de Tomaso's stroke, in tiny numbers with Ford V8s. Fewer than 50 cars were completed.
photoCaption: 1996 De Tomaso Guarà Coupé in Silver, front right
photoCredit: Photo: Mr.choppers, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Facel Vega
blurb: Jean Daninos turned a pressings company into France's last luxury marque: Chrysler V8s, hand-finished cabins, and a client list of kings and film stars. The Facellia's fragile engine sank the firm; production ended in October 1964.

name: HK500
intro: France's last great luxury GT at full strength: Jean Daninos's Facel Vega with a 6.3-litre Chrysler V8, a tubular chassis, and an interior finished like a Parisian salon, including the famous painted faux-wood dashboard, done by hand. Stirling Moss drove his across Europe between races.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Excellence
intro: A pillarless four-door hardtop on the grand scale, suicide rear doors, a Chrysler V8, and a price that bought several Citroën DSs. About 230 were built for kings, ambassadors and Ava Gardner; it remains the only French post-war car built to true American-limousine scale.
photoCaption: 1961 Facel Vega Excellence EX1, front left (Greenwich 2019)
photoCredit: Photo: Mr.choppers, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Facellia
intro: The little Facel, built to sell in volume with a twin-cam four designed by Carlo Marchisio, a jewel of an engine that proved fatally fragile in service and sank the company under warranty claims. Its successors (Facel III, with a Volvo engine, and the six-cylinder Facel 6) were the rescue attempt.
photoCredit: Photo: Rex Gray from Southern California, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Facel II
intro: Daninos called it the finest Facel of all, and the styling backs him: the HK500's successor cleaned the lines, stacked the headlamps, and kept the Chrysler power and the hand-finished cabin. Only 184 were built before Facel closed in October 1964.
photoCaption: 1963 Facel Vega Facel II from rear
photoCredit: Photo: MrWalkr, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Iso
blurb: Renzo Rivolta's company licensed the Isetta to BMW, then aimed the other way entirely: Bertone-bodied grand tourers with Chevrolet and Ford V8s. The Grifo is the peak, Bizzarrini engineering under one of the great GT shapes.

name: Rivolta IR 300
intro: Renzo Rivolta's move from Isetta bubble cars to a Corvette-engined GT: Bertone styling (by the young Giugiaro), a pressed-steel monocoque, De Dion rear suspension and Chevrolet's 327. The IR 340 raised the tune; about 800 Rivoltas were built.
photoCredit: Photo: Charles from Port Chester, New York, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Grifo
intro: The Rivolta formula turned up to supercar: Giotto Bizzarrini's chassis engineering, Bertone's most muscular coupé shape, and a ladder of Chevrolet and Ford V8s ending in the 7-litre big-block cars. The Grifo 7 Litri is Italy's answer to the Cobra question.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Fidia
intro: The four-door Iso, 'the fastest four seats in the world' in the advertising, and with a Corvette V8 up front the claim had substance. Ghia built the bodies; John Lennon bought one of the first. Fewer than 200 were made, first as the S4, then simply Fidia.
photoCredit: Photo: Riley from Christchurch, New Zealand, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Lele
intro: Iso's seventies GT, named for Renzo Rivolta's wife: a Marcello Gandini-penned 2+2 that began with Chevrolet power, moved to Ford's Cleveland, and carried the marque through its final decade. About 285 were built, including the Marlboro-sponsored Lele Sport specials.
photoCredit: Photo: Mr.choppers, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: NSU
blurb: A knitting-machine and motorcycle giant that bet the company on Felix Wankel's rotary engine: first in the little Spider, then in the Ro80, 1968's European Car of the Year. Engine warranties consumed NSU; Volkswagen absorbed it into Audi in 1969.

name: Prinz
intro: NSU's return to cars: a rear-engined two-cylinder runabout that grew, in the Prinz 4 of 1961, into the sharp-edged 'bathtub' saloon half of Germany learned to drive in. The Sport Prinz coupé (Bertone, styled by Franco Scaglione) proved the little chassis had glamour in it.
photoCredit: Photo: MrWalkr, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: 1000 / TT / TTS
intro: The Prinz grown up: a four-cylinder air-cooled saloon whose sporting derivatives, 1000 TT, 1200 TT and the twin-carburettor TTS, became the giant-killers of German hillclimbs and the car a generation of tuners (and the founders of Abt) learned on.
photoCredit: Photo: Rolf Heinrich, Köln, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Spider (Wankel Spider)
intro: The first production car in the world with a Wankel rotary engine: a Bertone-bodied roadster on the Sport Prinz chassis, its single-rotor engine spinning to speeds no piston twin could match. About 2,400 were built, and every rotary Mazda descends from the bet NSU placed here.
photoCredit: Photo: Andrew Bone from Weymouth, England, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Ro80
intro: European Car of the Year 1968 and the rotary's flagship: a twin-rotor saloon with front-wheel drive, a semi-automatic gearbox, inboard front discs and Claudio Luthe's wind-tunnel styling a decade ahead of the industry. The engine's seal problems bankrupted NSU into Volkswagen's arms, and the car itself was superb.
photoCredit: Photo: Rudolf Stricker, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Panhard
blurb: Panhard & Levassor set the automobile's layout in 1891, engine front, drive rear, then reinvented itself after the war around tiny air-cooled flat-twins, front-wheel drive and radical economy. Citroën absorbed the marque and ended its cars in 1967.

name: Dyna X
intro: Post-war France's cleverest small car: Jean-Albert Grégoire's aluminium-intensive design with Panhard's air-cooled flat-twin, front-wheel drive and room for a family on 610 cc. The Dyna X's light weight made it economical, quick for its class, and a rally winner.
photoCaption: 1952 Panhard Dyna X 120 Canadienne in Bremen, front left
photoCredit: Photo: Andrew Bone from Weymouth, England, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Dyna Z
intro: The Dyna X's successor traded aluminium for steel as costs bit, kept the flat-twin and front-drive, and gained Louis Bionier's rounded 'ponton' styling with a panoramic windscreen. The Tigre versions are the sporting cars, with the twin tuned and the chassis sorted.
photoCredit: Photo: Saruman, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

name: PL 17
intro: The Dyna Z evolved: named for Panhard-Levassor and its 17 tax-and-space formula, restyled with a droop snoot and eyelid headlamps, and crowned by a Monte Carlo Rally outright win in 1961, three PL 17s in the top places, against the factories of Europe.
photoCredit: Photo: Herranderssvensson, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: 24 CT / BT
intro: Panhard's last car: a steel-bodied coupé (and rare saloon) styled by Louis Bionier with the flat-twin behind a long, low nose, named for the 24 Hours its makers dreamed of, where the related CD coupés had already won the Index of Performance. Citroën, which had absorbed Panhard, ended car production in 1967.
photoCredit: Photo: Arnaud 25, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Simca
blurb: Founded to build Fiats in France, Simca became the country's second carmaker on the Aronde, bought Ford's French V8 works, pioneered the hatchback with the 1100, and faded through Chrysler and Peugeot ownership by 1970.

name: Aronde
intro: The swallow (hirondelle, hence the badge) that made Simca France's second carmaker: a modern monocoque saloon with the Flash engine, sold in everything from taxi trim to the elegant Facel-built coupés. Over 1.4 million were made.
photoCredit: Photo: Philmarin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Vedette
intro: Ford of France's V8, inherited whole when Simca bought the Poissy plant in 1954: a flathead 2.4-litre V8 in an American-styled saloon, Versailles, Trianon, Régence, then the Présidence and the Chambord. France's last V8-engined production car of its era, and the seed of Brazil's Simca do Brasil.
photoCredit: Photo: Rutger van der Maar, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

intro: Simca's rear-engined answer to the Renault 4 and the Beetle era: a square-cut four-door with the Poissy engine behind the rear axle, built for seventeen years and rallied hard in its Rallye forms, the Rallye 2 and 3 are homologation-bred tarmac weapons with a cult following.
photoCredit: Photo: Wleiter, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

intro: One of the first true hatchbacks: transverse engine, front-wheel drive, a folding rear seat and a hatch, years before the Golf defined the class. The 1100 Ti and the Matra-Simca Rancho (the leisure off-roader it sired) show the range's reach; nearly 2.9 million were built.
photoCredit: Photo: Charles01, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Talbot-Lago
blurb: Anthony Lago took over Talbot's French works and built the summit of the French classics: Figoni-teardrop coupés before the war, a Le Mans winner after it. The America of 1955 was the last car; Simca absorbed the firm in 1959.

name: T150C-SS
intro: Anthony Lago's Talbot at its zenith: the T150C chassis with Wilson pre-selector gearbox and a 4.0-litre six, clothed by Figoni & Falaschi in the famous 'goutte d'eau' teardrop coupés, the most valuable French cars of the thirties, and regular concours Best-of-Show winners today.
photoCredit: Photo: Joe Ross from Lansing, Michigan, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: T26 Record / Grand Sport
intro: Post-war Talbot-Lago: the 4.5-litre twin-cam six in the Record saloon and the short-chassis Grand Sport, one of the fastest road cars of its day and a Le Mans winner in 1950 (a T26 GS, father and son Rosier driving). Grand Sport chassis went to the great coachbuilders, Saoutchik, Figoni, Franay.
photoCredit: Photo: Rutger van der Maar, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: T14 America
intro: The last Talbot-Lago: a small coupé that began with Talbot's own 2.5-litre four and ended, as money ran out, with BMW's 2.6-litre V8 and the America name. About 120 were built; Simca bought the company in 1959 and the marque slept until the name resurfaced under Peugeot in 1979.
photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Willys
blurb: Willys-Overland built the wartime Jeep and spent the peace turning it civilian: the CJ, the all-steel station wagon that prefigured the SUV, and the Aero saloon. Kaiser bought the company in 1953; the Willys name left its grilles in the 1960s.

name: MB (Willys Jeep)
intro: The Jeep: Willys-Overland's MB (built alongside Ford's near-identical GPW) put over 360,000 Willys examples into every theatre of the Second World War on the 60 hp Go Devil four. It is the most consequential utility vehicle ever made, and the ancestor of everything in this atlas with seven grille slots.
photoCaption: Wartime Jeep (MB pattern) with trailer, front 3/4
photoCredit: Photo: Greg Gjerdingen from Willmar, USA, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: CJ (Civilian Jeep)
intro: The Jeep comes home: the CJ-2A of 1945 put the wartime formula to farm and trail work, and the line ran for four decades, CJ-3B's high hood, the CJ-5's twenty-year production, the CJ-7's extra room and the Scrambler's pickup bed. Willys built them until 1963; Kaiser and AMC carried the line on.
photoCredit: Photo: Medium69, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Station Wagon / Pickup
intro: America's first all-steel station wagon, Brooks Stevens's design sold the Jeep idea to families, and the same bones carried the pickup truck and panel delivery. Four-wheel drive from 1949 made it the original SUV in all but name, a decade and a half before the term.
photoCredit: Photo: kalacaw, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Aero
intro: Willys's post-war passenger car: a light, efficient unitary saloon (Aero Lark, Wing, Ace and the Eagle hardtop) that handled well, sipped fuel and sold against the full weight of the Big Three. Production moved to Brazil, where the Aero Willys lived on into the 1970s.
photoCaption: 1954 Willys Aero Eagle Hardtop, front right (Hershey 2019)
photoCredit: Photo: Mr.choppers, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
